s.en: The Academy sent its students home before it was much past noon.
The Great Clock Tower was sealed off, military police stood at the main gate, and a single curt notice went up on the board: "Accident caused by the fall of an aged component."
No one had died, no one was badly hurt, so as accidents went it was a small one — or at least, that was the version the Academy seemed to want.
In the lift going back down to the lower ring, Sera didn't take the pocket watch out once.
She didn't need to. She knew.
Deep in her breast pocket it went on ticking out its backward beat, regular as a pulse.
Tick, tick — as though it were counting something back down.
When she got back to the shop, Oz was out.
On the workbench lay a note in his gruff hand: "Buying parts. Back by evening."
Sera flung down her bag, ran up to the attic, locked the door, and only then set the watch on her desk.
Looking again, she saw that fine graduations had surfaced around the rim of the dial, markings that hadn't been visible that morning.
A small ring divided into twelve, much finer than the numerals outside it.
Each time the second hand stepped backward, one division of the ring glowed a faint blue, then went dark.
Holding her breath, Sera set a finger on the crown.
On an ordinary pocket watch, you turned this to wind the mainspring.
But with this watch, there was something she simply had to try.
She flicked one of the gears off the edge of the desk and let it drop to the floor.
A dry clatter.
At the same moment, she twisted the crown the wrong way.
Her vision warped like soft wax.
The gear bouncing on the floor retraced the arc it had just drawn, rose back into the air, and settled neatly onto the edge of the desk.
Her fingertip still held the vivid feel of having just flicked it.
"...It went back."
The moment she said it aloud, her knees buckled.
Clinging to the desk, she somehow got herself down onto the floor.
Her heart was hammering as if she'd just sprinted up a hill.
When she wiped under her nose, something red and slick came away on the back of her hand.
A nosebleed.
"...So it doesn't come free."
She tried it a few more times, and learned a few things.
She could turn back ten seconds at most.
Every time, heat was drawn from the core of her body, and on the third try the world nearly went black.
And it seemed she was the only one who remembered time going back.
The pigeon that crossed the window flew the same path twice and disappeared beyond the rooftops without noticing a thing.
For ten years she'd thought of it as nothing more than a keepsake.
What it really was, Sera hadn't the faintest idea.
If one thing was certain, it was this: her mother must have known what it was.
The bell over the shop door rang downstairs just as the sky outside had turned fully to madder red.
"I'm back."
At the familiar rasp, Sera scrubbed the traces of blood off with her sleeve before heading down the stairs.
Oz was laying out oilpaper parcels on the workbench, and spoke without looking up.
"Heard there was an accident up at the Academy. The rumour's trickled all the way down here."
"Yeah. A gear came down... but nobody got hurt."
"Well, that's the main thing."
Seeing that her grandfather's hands showed no sign of stopping, Sera hesitated.
Should she tell him, or keep quiet?
In the end she took the watch from her breast pocket and laid it gently on the workbench.
"Grandpa. Look at this."
The instant he saw the second hand running backwards, the colour drained from Oz's face.
The tweezers between his fingers clattered onto the workbench.
Fingertips that had never once trembled in forty years, however tiny the part, were trembling now.
"...So it moved."
"Today, in the tower. And then I—"
Sera told him everything that had happened, every last bit of it.
The world that stopped. The gear that rewound. Saving Viola Eisen. And what she had just confirmed up in the attic.
Oz listened to the end without a word.
Even after she'd finished, he didn't open his mouth for a while.
The wall clock struck six, and as the last chime soaked into the corners of the shop and was gone, he finally let out a long sigh.
"That Elise... so it finally came true."
"'Came true'... Grandpa, do you know something?"
"Not enough to call it knowing."
Oz thrust a hand into the very back of a workbench drawer.
What he brought out was a small brass key wrapped in an oil-stained cloth.
Carved into the bow of the key was the same crest as on the watch lid.
"Your mother — she wasn't just a clockmaker's girl."
"Up till ten years ago she worked as an engineer at the Great Clock Tower. Hired by House Eisen."
"House Eisen... Viola's family?"
"The night before she disappeared, she left this key with me, and she said—"
"'If that watch ever starts moving again, give this to Sera. Until then, don't tell her anything.'"
Sera took the key.
It fit in her palm, and yet it felt heavy.
"Why didn't you ever tell me?"
"Once you've given your word, you keep it. That's what a craftsman is."
Oz tossed out the words gruffly and turned back to his parts.
But his back looked a little smaller than usual, and it surely wasn't her imagination.
"...Do you think Mom's still alive?"
There was no answer.
Only the small sound of him taking up the tweezers again echoed through the hushed shop.
The next morning, wherever you went in the Academy, the accident was all anyone talked about.

The gear that fell was the size of a house; no, the whole tower had tilted; apparently someone in Chronomancy had used a forbidden art — with every passing in the corridors, the story grew fins and tails and swelled.
Sera's name was mixed in there too.
"They say some Mechanics scholarship girl shoved Lady Eisen."
"Not shoved — saved, surely?"
"Either way, how on earth did she start running before it fell?"
She had saved a life, and far from being praised, she was apparently under suspicion.
Half-hiding her face behind her textbook, Sera hurried towards Mechanics' shabby workshop building.
She didn't regret saving her.
But she hated drawing attention. Above all, she had to avoid, at any cost, anyone catching on about that watch.
Just as she reached the covered walkway to the workshops, a voice called from behind her.
"Miss Milford. Might I have a moment of your time?"
She didn't need to turn around.
Viola Eisen stood there without a single hanger-on.
As though yesterday's dust had been a lie, her silver hair was pinned up without a strand out of place.
"...I've got workshop now, actually."

t: お伝えしておきました
s.en: "I am aware. I have already informed Instructor Regen myself."
Her tone allowed no argument.
Viola set off without waiting for a reply, and Sera, with no other option, followed.
Where she was taken was a glass-walled greenhouse at the far end of the Chronomancy grounds.
The instant she stepped inside, Sera stopped short.
Every flower in bloom was one she had never seen.
Roses going from bud to full bloom, from full bloom to withering and falling, over and over every few seconds.
Lilies whose petals hung motionless in midair, caught partway through falling.
"It is the Chronomancy course's practice greenhouse. Here, no one will overhear us."
Viola stopped by a small iron table and turned to face Sera.
"I shall be direct. That day, you turned back time. Did you not?"
Her heart leapt.
"...What are you talking about?"
"Playing innocent is pointless."
Viola snapped her fan shut.
"We chronomancers feel the flow of time on our skin. The way, in water, you can tell which way the current runs."
"In that instant, time inside the tower twisted and ran backwards. And at the centre of that whirlpool stood you."

t: ごまかしようがなかった
s.en: There was no way to talk her way out of it.
Sera gave in and set the pocket watch on the table.
Watching the second hand run backwards, Viola's eyes narrowed.
"And the crest on the lid... So it is as I thought."
"You know this crest?"
"I have seen it once. At the back of my father's study — in a scorched old document kept in a locked bookcase."
Viola lowered her voice.
"A hundred years ago there were chronomancers called Rewinders. Not stoppers of time, nor hasteners — the one and only bloodline that could turn it back."
"Yet from a certain day on, every last one of them vanishes from the records. Names, lineages, everything."
"All that remained was that crest and a single line: 'The followers of Reversal are hereby forbidden.'"
Somewhere in the greenhouse, another rose bloomed and fell.
"Wait. Then my mom was..."
"Quite possibly of Rewinder blood. And so, then, are you."
"But I don't even have a sigil."
"That is precisely what I cannot make sense of."
Viola bit her lip for a while, then lifted her head as if she'd made up her mind.

t: お話ししておかなければならない
s.en: "Miss Milford. There is one more thing I must tell you."
"The time crystal is dying."
"...What?"
"That was the third time this month a time-tremor has struck. Yesterday's was the largest by far."
"If the light keeps fading like this, sooner or later time in Vern will stop. Not for an instant, like yesterday. Forever."
"But... what does the Academy say?"
"Nothing. My father and the Rector both insist it's 'merely a temporary malfunction', and won't budge."
For the first time, frustration seeped into Viola's voice.
"Guarding the Great Clock is the duty of House Eisen. So long as my father refuses to admit it, I have no choice but to act myself."
"So that's why you came to me?"
"Yes. Your watch may well be a clue to something. And besides—"
Viola abruptly looked away.
"Leaving a debt for my life unpaid goes against my principles."
Not one for straight answers, Sera thought.
Still, it felt somehow different from yesterday's thorniness.
"I've got one condition."
"...And that would be?"
"Niko's in too. I'm bad at secrets. He's the one person I won't lie to."
Viola frowned without bothering to hide it.
"That noisy gentleman with the merchant's twang?"
"He's good. When it comes to machines, he knows more than anyone at the Academy."
After a long silence, Viola gave a small nod with every appearance of profound reluctance.
"...Very well. Now that we are allies, kindly do not hold me back."
After school, the three of them met at the warehouse Niko rented.
Half of the old canal-side warehouse was occupied by the half-built flying machine.
Wings of stretched sailcloth, a body that was all patches, and, hanging from a ceiling beam, an engine of uncertain nature.
Viola stopped in the doorway and covered her nose and mouth with a lace handkerchief.
"...Do people actually live here?"
"Nobody lives here. It's a workshop. A workshop."
Niko laughed and waved a greasy hand.
"Man, I never thought you'd actually bring Her Ladyship. What kind of magic trick did you pull?"
"Not a trick exactly... it's, well, a long story."
Sera summed up everything so far.
The watch. Her grandfather's story. What she'd heard in the greenhouse, about the Rewinders and the time crystal.
When she'd finished, Niko, unusually, didn't crack a joke; he folded his arms.
"Right, I see. And this is the key, then."
Niko took the brass key, held it up to the light slanting in through the window, and narrowed his eyes.
"This here's a maintenance key."
"Maintenance key?"
"My old man used to haul cargo in the service tunnels under the canals. The keys to those doors were exactly this shape."
"Under the lower ring there's loads of old tunnels that go all the way to the roots of the Great Clock Tower. Most of 'em are sealed off now, mind."
"The roots... of the Great Clock Tower."
Viola drew a sharp little breath.
"Beneath the tower lies the foundation that bears the time crystal. Yet even among House Eisen, only my father is permitted to enter."
"And a way to it, down in the lower ring..."
The three of them looked at one another.
None of them said it, but they were all thinking the same thing.
"Just sayin' — if we're going, we've gotta prepare properly."
When Niko said this with a straight face, Viola gave a little sniff.
"Oh my, how unexpected. I had taken you for the type who leaps in first."
"Oh, I'll leap in. After I've prepared."
At the two of them, plainly on different wavelengths or maybe exactly the same one, Sera burst out laughing.
Yesterday morning, she'd never have imagined any of this.
No — imagining was the least of it: a day when she'd sit around the same table as Viola Eisen hadn't crossed her mind even in her dreams.
That night.
Coming down after turning off the shop lights to check the locks, Sera noticed something white wedged under the door.
An envelope.
No addressee, no sender. It was sealed with grey wax, and pressed into the wax was that crest.
With trembling fingers, Sera broke the seal.
Inside was a single thin sheet of letter paper.
"Tomorrow night, 3:17. I will wait at the old No. 7 Maintenance Gate."
Beneath it, in place of a signature, a single letter.
Elise. Her mother's initial.
She couldn't help suspecting a trap.
If it really was her mother, why ten years of silence? Why now?
And yet, even as she thought it, she couldn't stop the heat rising helplessly in her chest.
In her breast pocket, the watch went on ticking, backwards.
